The problem is that the only way for Claude to interpret or perceive the game is through screenshots or text output in headless mode which are both insufficient and inherently non-realtime. Maybe we could build an agent that can process the game data directly somehow and translate it to Claude since Claude is an LLM, like we build an interpreter? This is a fascinating problem — bridging an LLM's text-native perception with a real-time game engine's structured state. Let me launch a deep research dive into this. I'll cover MCP-based game integrations, structured game-state serialization protocols, agentic frameworks that bypass screenshot-based perception, real-time streaming architectures, and novel approaches for making Claude Code a first-class participant in your engine loop.

Starting the deep dive now.

Your research report on bridging Claude Code to your real-time voxel engine is ready. It covers MCP protocol implementation with the official C# SDK, structured game state serialization best practices from Voyager and related research, the three-layer reactive/tactical/strategic architecture for handling the LLM-to-game-loop latency gap, and practical guidance for building an MCP server exposing your ECS. The report also surveys agentic framework findings, Claude Code's Channels feature for bidirectional push notifications, and emerging approaches like active inference and RAG over game history relevant to The Infinite Labyrinth.
This is for the Rust based project not the C# project.

I want to make sure I target the right project — let me check what we've discussed about your Rust work.

Got it — the Rust-based Infinite Labyrinth at `[redacted:local-path]`, not the deprecated C# one. That changes the implementation layer significantly — Rust MCP SDK, different crate ecosystem, different interop patterns. Let me pull up the project structure to ground this properly.

Good, I have full context on the Rust project now — the 6-crate workspace with `il_voxel`, `il_world`, `il_sim`, `il_data`, wgpu rendering, 5cm voxel resolution, material-first ECS. Let me research the Rust-specific MCP ecosystem and rewrite this properly.

Now I have everything I need. Let me build the Rust-specific version of this report, grounded in your actual crate workspace and the Rust MCP/LLM ecosystem.

Here's the Rust-specific research report, fully grounded in your actual workspace architecture.

The big picture: add an `il_mcp` crate to your workspace using the official `rmcp` v0.16.0 SDK. The MCP server communicates with your game loop via `tokio::sync::watch` (snapshots) and `mpsc` (commands) — the game loop never blocks. Claude Code connects to this server via stdio transport, gets structured semantic access to your ECS through 10-15 focused tools, and operates as a "slow strategic mind" on a 2-5 second cycle while your game runs at 60 FPS.

The novel ideas I'm most excited about for your project specifically:

**Material-aware affordances** — Claude doesn't see "a door," it sees "oak door (flash_point: 250°C, tensile: 0.4)" and reasons about what's possible. No other game-AI system derives perception from material properties. Your "Everything is Material" philosophy becomes Claude's reasoning substrate.

**Active inference escalation** — don't poll Claude every 3 seconds regardless. Use prediction error (surprise) to decide WHEN to escalate. Routine gameplay stays local. Novel encounters, unexpected material interactions, narrative inflection points trigger Claude. This is dramatically more token-efficient.

**Dual-model hybrid** — `llama-cpp-2` running Qwen 2.5 1.5B locally for 50ms tactical decisions, Claude API for 2,000ms strategic decisions. Best of both worlds.

The implementation roadmap starts with a 1-2 week foundation (5 read-only tools, channel bridge, snapshot publishing) and builds toward the full intelligent architecture over 6-12 weeks total.

What can we do with the code dimensionally or topologically? It still feels like we are chasing after the coattails of other games when we could be innovating with the tech and code. Are voxels the best for IL? Most efficient?

This is the right question. Let me dig deep into the math and CS that could make IL's representation genuinely novel rather than "Minecraft but finer."

Now I have enough to synthesize something genuinely novel. Let me think through this carefully because the question deserves more than a survey — it deserves new ideas.

You're asking exactly the right question. The answer is: **no, cubic voxels are not the best representation for a game called The Infinite Labyrinth — and the name itself tells you why.** A labyrinth is fundamentally a *topological* object. Its power comes from how spaces *connect*, not from the shape of the spaces themselves. Voxels on a cubic lattice have the most boring topology possible — trivially contractible, no handles, no non-contractible loops. You're building a universe-scale structure out of sugar cubes.

Let me show the design space first, then go deep.

Now let me unpack each axis and explain what becomes possible when you move along them.

---

**The cubic voxel grid is a terrible fit for 5cm resolution.** At 5cm, a single 1-meter doorway is 20×40×20 = 16,000 voxels. A modest 100m×100m terrain chunk is 2000×2000×200 = 800 million voxels. Even with palette compression (2 bytes each), that's 1.6 GB for one chunk. This is why Minecraft uses 1m voxels — the math only works at coarse resolution with flat arrays. At 5cm, you *must* use a sparse hierarchical structure.

The proven solution is the **Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (SVDAG)** — a generalization of the Sparse Voxel Octree where identical subtrees are merged into a single node. A binary voxel grid can be represented orders of magnitude more efficiently using an SVDAG than a traditional SVO by exploiting repeating geometric patterns. At 5cm resolution, repeating geometry is everywhere — every stretch of uniform stone wall, every section of identical flooring, every run of air. The symmetry-aware variant (SSVDAG) further improves compression by also detecting mirror-symmetric subtrees. In your Rust workspace, this maps to replacing flat voxel arrays in `il_voxel` with an SVDAG structure — the `voxel-rs` project on GitHub already demonstrates an SVO raytracer in Rust with wgpu that achieves interactive framerates on infinite terrain.

But compression alone doesn't answer your real question. You're asking whether the *primitive itself* is right.

---

**The deeper problem: a voxel is geometry without physics.** A cubic voxel says "this location is filled with material X." That's it. It has no concept of surface normal, no sub-voxel detail, no smooth boundary. Your material system has 13 axes of variation per material — tensile strength, conductivity, acid resistance, flash point — but the geometry holding those materials is jagged cubes. There's a representational mismatch.

The hybrid that solves this: **SDF geometry + discrete material identity.** Store material as a voxel attribute (discrete material ID per cell), but store *shape* as a signed distance field (continuous function per cell giving distance-to-surface). This is essentially what Teardown does internally, and it's why Teardown looks dramatically better than Minecraft at similar voxel density. The SDF gives you smooth surfaces, sub-voxel precision, free surface normals (just take the gradient), and natural LOD (just sample the SDF at a coarser resolution). The material ID gives you your "Everything is Material" semantics. In your wgsl shader, ray marching through an SDF is actually *simpler* than traditional voxel rendering — sphere tracing naturally skips empty space.

In Rust this means each chunk stores two parallel fields: a `Vec<f16>` for SDF values (distance to nearest surface) and a `Vec<u16>` for material IDs. Surface extraction for physics/collision uses marching cubes on the SDF. Rendering uses ray marching. Material interaction queries look up the material ID. Total memory is comparable to pure voxels but you get dramatically richer geometry.

---

Now the truly novel stuff. Everything above is optimization. This is where IL can become something no other game is.

**The labyrinth should have impossible topology.** Right now your chunks connect to their 6 face-neighbors in a flat Euclidean grid. Walk north from chunk (0,0,0) and you reach (0,1,0). Always. Predictably. But a labyrinth's entire identity is that *the space itself is treacherous*. What if chunks had an *adjacency override table*?

```rust
pub struct ChunkTopology {
    /// Standard Euclidean neighbors (computed from position)
    euclidean: [ChunkId; 6],
    /// Overridden adjacency — when set, replaces the Euclidean neighbor
    /// This is how you build impossible spaces
    portal: [Option<(ChunkId, Transform)>; 6],
}
```

Walk north from a corridor and you emerge on the *ceiling* of a chamber three realms away. Walk through a doorway and the room behind you is no longer the room you came from. This isn't portals-as-game-mechanic (like *Portal*) — this is the *fundamental connectivity of the world*. The labyrinth isn't built in Euclidean space with portals bolted on. The labyrinth IS a non-trivially-connected manifold, and the chunk adjacency graph IS its topology.

HyperRogue has been doing this for over a decade — a roguelike set in genuine hyperbolic geometry where the space genuinely expands exponentially as you move away from center. Its RogueViz engine supports two-dimensional hyperbolic, Euclidean, and spherical geometry, product geometries, twisted geometries (Nil, Solv), and Thurston geometries. The key insight from ZenoRogue's work: non-Euclidean spaces feel *profoundly alien* without any visual trickery. The geometry itself is the horror, or the wonder, or the divinity. Your omniversal concept — each realm having a completely different genre and aesthetic — maps perfectly to each realm having a different *metric tensor*.

A horror realm uses hyperbolic geometry: rooms get bigger as you go deeper, corridors branch exponentially, you can never retrace your path because the space literally has more volume the further you go. A divine realm uses spherical geometry: walk far enough in any direction and you return to where you started, because the universe is closed and finite. A cyberpunk realm uses flat geometry with non-trivial topology: the city loops on itself like a torus, every alley connects to every other alley through an adjacency web.

The rendering is the same for all of them — ray marching through your SDF — but the ray marching step applies the realm's metric to compute distance. In hyperbolic space, parallel rays diverge. In spherical space, they converge. Your wgsl shader already does ray marching. Making it non-Euclidean is changing one function: `fn step_ray(pos, dir, metric) -> (new_pos, new_dir)`.

---

**The fiber bundle architecture maps your cosmology to code.** Your philosophical framework treats reality as layered — Thought → Energy → Matter → Organized Process → Thought². Your omniversal game has realms stacked on a base labyrinth. This IS a fiber bundle.

In mathematics, a fiber bundle is a space E that locally looks like a product B × F (base × fiber) but globally may be twisted. The base space B is the labyrinth itself — the skeletal graph of rooms and corridors that constitutes the meta-structure connecting all realms. The fiber F at each point is the realm's actual geometry — the detailed voxels/SDF that makes up the world you walk through. The structure group G governs transitions between fibers — when you cross a realm boundary, the transition function rotates your orientation, rescales your size, remaps your material interactions.

```rust
pub struct RealmTransition {
    /// How spatial coordinates transform at the boundary
    pub spatial: Mat4,
    /// How material properties remap (iron in cyberpunk realm → nanometal in sci-fi realm)
    pub material_map: HashMap<MaterialId, MaterialId>,
    /// How the metric tensor changes (flat → hyperbolic → spherical)
    pub metric_transition: MetricInterpolation,
    /// Transition duration in chunks (how many chunks to blend over)
    pub blend_width: u32,
}
```

The labyrinth's "base space" can be a low-dimensional graph structure — rooms as nodes, corridors as edges — that you can procedurally generate, analyze topologically (compute fundamental group, homology), and guarantee properties like "every realm is reachable" and "no dead-end realms" through graph-theoretic constraints. This separates the *structure* of the labyrinth from the *content* of the realms, letting you reason about both independently.

---

**The material axis as a genuine extra dimension.** Here's an idea that synthesizes your "Everything is Material" philosophy with higher-dimensional thinking, without going full Miegakure. Instead of 4D spatial voxels (computationally brutal — 4D at 5cm is 160,000 voxels per cubic meter *per slice*), give each voxel a *material phase coordinate*.

Think of it as: every point in space exists along a continuum from "most physical" (phase=0) to "most ethereal" (phase=1). Most objects exist at phase=0 — solid, normal. But Ascended items have non-zero phase extent. A sword that has been through the Coherence Engine might exist from phase 0.0 to phase 0.3 — it has presence in the ethereal dimension that normal items lack. An entity could "phase shift" to see the same room at a different material depth, where walls might be transparent and hidden structures become visible.

This isn't rendering trick — it's a real axis in your SDF. Each voxel stores `sdf: f16, material_id: u16, phase_extent: u8`. Ray marching samples the SDF at the player's current phase coordinate. The cost is a single extra lookup per step, not the exponential blowup of true 4D.

---

So to answer your questions directly:

**Are voxels the best for IL?** No. A *hybrid* of SVDAG (for spatial hierarchy and compression), SDF (for sub-voxel geometry and smooth surfaces), and discrete material IDs (for your 13-axis material system) is dramatically better. You keep voxel-like interaction semantics (place a block, mine a block) but gain smooth surfaces, 100× compression, and natural LOD — all critical at 5cm resolution.

**Most efficient?** SVDAG is the state of the art for sparse voxel storage — achieving average storage efficiencies of about 5 bytes per occupied voxel, with the transform-aware SVDAG (2025) further exploiting mirror symmetries. The Aokana framework (2025) demonstrated GPU-driven open-world rendering at interactive rates using SVDAG with DAG-based geometry compression. In Rust, this maps cleanly to your existing octree-adjacent thinking.

**What can we do dimensionally/topologically?** This is where IL can be genuinely unprecedented:

The **portal topology** layer — where chunks have overridable adjacency — gives you impossible labyrinth spaces that no other voxel game has attempted. The **fiber bundle** structure separates the labyrinth's *skeleton* from each realm's *flesh*, letting you procedurally generate topologically guaranteed labyrinth structures (no dead ends, every realm reachable, specific homological properties) independently from the voxel content. The **per-realm metric tensor** gives each genre its own spatial character without any visual gimmicks — hyperbolic horror, spherical divinity, toroidal cyberpunk — and the cost in your shader is one function swap in the ray marching loop. The **material phase axis** extends your "Everything is Material" philosophy into an extra pseudo-dimension that Ascended items occupy, giving the Coherence Engine physical-geometric meaning rather than just a score.

None of these exist in any shipping game. Minecraft has flat cubic grids. Teardown has SDF voxels but flat topology. HyperRogue has non-Euclidean geometry but no material system. Miegakure has 4D but no procedural generation. IL could be the first to combine hierarchical SDF geometry, non-trivial topological connectivity, per-realm curvature, and a material-phase dimension — and your Rust/wgpu stack is actually the right foundation for it, because all of this ultimately reduces to "how do you step a ray through structured data on a GPU."

Want me to spec out any of these layers in implementation detail — the SVDAG crate architecture, the portal topology chunk system, the metric-aware ray marcher, or the phase axis integration?

Why even represent the world as blocks? Let me ask this, what's the most performative and efficient and visually pleasing way to procedurally generate and render the world? We aren't going to have block placing or building, it's an action RPG/Roguelike. I wanted voxels because I wanted everything generated mathematically/algorithmically instead of hand creating assets and I thought voxels would be easiest to get something that looks good but it's bad. 

So we need a completely novel way to procedurally generate not only the world and elaborate structures, entities, items, but also a novel way to render them. Computationally efficient. 

In fact, we can add some constraints, we don't need nor want infinitely expanding worlds we want interesting environments that can evolve and interact.

This changes everything. If you don't need block placement, *the entire reason voxels exist in games disappears.* Voxels are a storage format for player-editable worlds. You're not making a builder — you're making an action RPG. You need procedural generation and beautiful rendering. Those are two different problems with a shared solution that is NOT voxels.

Let me research the actual state of the art for fully procedural worlds without discrete grids.

Now I have the full picture. Let me lay out the architecture that replaces voxels entirely.

Now let me explain why this is transformative for IL specifically, beyond just "SDF looks better."

**The world doesn't exist until you look at it.** With voxels, you generate a chunk and store it — 800 million values sitting in memory whether anyone's looking or not. With pure SDF, the world is a *function*. It produces geometry on demand, pixel by pixel, frame by frame. A room that nobody is looking at costs *zero memory and zero compute*. This is exactly the constraint you just described — bounded, interesting environments rather than infinite expanding worlds. The room exists as a 1KB operation tree. It only becomes *visible geometry* when a ray hits it.

**Destruction and evolution are first-class operations.** Want to blow a hole in a wall? Subtract a sphere SDF from the wall SDF: `smooth_subtraction(wall, sphere(explosion_center, blast_radius), blend_k)`. The wall now has a smooth, organic crater. No re-meshing, no chunk updates, no edge cases. Want erosion over time? Increase the blend parameter on the subtraction operations that define corridors, making them wider and smoother. Want a living dungeon that grows? Add new union operations to the SDF tree — stalactites descending, walls narrowing, new passages opening. The SDF tree IS the world state, and modifying the tree IS modifying the world.

**Your material system drives the visuals directly.** This is where "Everything is Material" becomes visually profound. When the ray marcher hits a surface, it has the material ID. Your 13-axis material properties become shader parameters: `conductivity` maps to metallic reflection, `brittleness` maps to surface micro-roughness (cracked vs smooth), `flash_point` creates heat shimmer near fires, `acid_resistance` maps to surface corrosion patterns (domain-warped noise masked by the acid field). The material IS the texture. No UV mapping, no texture artists, no hand-painting. A corroding iron door looks different from a corroding bronze door because the material properties feed different noise frequencies and color ramps into the shader.

**Entities as animated SDF skeletons.** Inigo Quilez demonstrated procedural animated creatures in Shadertoy — a character built entirely from SDF primitives with smooth blending, animated by transforming bone positions. For IL, a procedural creature generator outputs a parameterized skeleton: number of limbs, limb segment lengths, joint radii, body proportions, head shape — all fed into an SDF composition function. A spider is 8 capsule-limbs smooth-blended into an ellipsoid body with sphere eyes. A dragon is a chain of spheres (spine) with capsule ribs and membrane surfaces (thin boxes between rib endpoints). The material system tells you what the creature LOOKS like — chitin has a specific roughness and subsurface scattering profile, scale has a specific anisotropic reflection. You don't model creatures. You *parameterize* them and the math does the rest.

**The portal topology from the previous discussion works even better here.** With voxels, portal stitching requires careful chunk boundary management. With SDF ray marching, a portal is literally just: when the ray crosses the portal plane, transform its position and direction into the target space and continue marching. That's one matrix multiply mid-march. The ray doesn't care that it just teleported — it's still marching through a distance function. Non-Euclidean geometry is equally trivial: modify the step function to apply the realm's metric tensor. Hyperbolic space, spherical space, flat-with-portals — all just different `fn step(pos, dir, metric) -> (new_pos, new_dir)` implementations.

**The performance story is better than you'd think.** The concern with SDF ray marching has always been "it's slower than rasterization." This was true in 2015. It's increasingly false in 2026. GPUs have grown their compute-to-bandwidth ratio dramatically — modern GPUs have 10-50 TFLOPS of compute but memory bandwidth hasn't kept pace. SDF ray marching is *pure compute* — it reads essentially no memory (the SDF tree is tiny, fits in cache). Rasterization is memory-bandwidth-bound (vertex buffers, index buffers, textures, framebuffers). As Quilez observed, GPUs have been evolving their compute capabilities faster than their memory bandwidth, making pure mathematical SDFs increasingly competitive against stored representations. A two-tier BVH over SDF groups — where the first tier does cheap AABB tests to cull distant primitives and the second tier evaluates only relevant SDFs — keeps the per-pixel cost bounded regardless of total scene complexity. Recent work on recursive SDF rendering and cone marching further reduces the per-pixel cost by sharing work between neighboring pixels.

Here's what the Rust architecture looks like:

The critical thing to understand about this architecture: **the SDF operation tree IS the world format.** Generation outputs a tree. Rendering reads the tree. Simulation mutates the tree. There's no intermediate representation — no voxels, no meshes, no point clouds. The tree is tiny (a complex room might be 500 SDF nodes, each ~32 bytes, so ~16KB), resolution-independent (the same tree renders at 480p on a laptop and 4K on a desktop), and trivially serializable (save/load a dungeon floor is saving/loading a tree).

The `il_sdf` crate is the foundation — it defines the node types:

```rust
pub enum SDFNode {
    // Primitives
    Sphere { center: Vec3, radius: f32 },
    Box { center: Vec3, half_extents: Vec3, rounding: f32 },
    Capsule { a: Vec3, b: Vec3, radius: f32 },
    Torus { center: Vec3, major_r: f32, minor_r: f32 },
    Cylinder { a: Vec3, b: Vec3, radius: f32 },

    // CSG operations
    Union { children: Vec<NodeId> },
    Subtract { base: NodeId, cutter: NodeId },
    Intersect { a: NodeId, b: NodeId },
    SmoothUnion { children: Vec<NodeId>, k: f32 },
    SmoothSubtract { base: NodeId, cutter: NodeId, k: f32 },

    // Domain operations
    Repeat { child: NodeId, period: Vec3 },     // Infinite repetition
    Twist { child: NodeId, strength: f32 },
    Bend { child: NodeId, axis: Axis, k: f32 },
    Warp { child: NodeId, noise_params: NoiseParams },

    // Material assignment
    WithMaterial { child: NodeId, material_id: MaterialId },

    // Transform
    Transform { child: NodeId, matrix: Mat4 },
}
```

This is the entire geometric vocabulary. A dungeon room, a dragon, a magic sword, a mountain — they're all trees of these nodes. The `il_gen` crate composes them procedurally. The `il_render` crate compiles them to wgsl and ray marches them. Nothing else exists.

What makes this *genuinely novel for a shipping game*: Dreams used SDF but converted to point clouds for rendering. Shadertoy demos use pure SDF ray marching but for single static scenes. Nobody has built a full action RPG where the world, entities, items, destruction, and evolution are all unified under a single SDF operation tree architecture. The closest thing is the demoscene, where entire worlds fit in 64 kilobytes of code — because SDF is *the most information-dense representation of geometry that exists.* Your game would be the first to take that demoscene insight and build a real game engine around it.

The bounded-world constraint you just added makes this even more tractable. You don't need infinite terrain streaming. You have a dungeon floor, a realm, a bounded arena — all small enough that their SDF trees fit comfortably in GPU memory. Evolution and interaction happen by mutating the tree. And when the player moves to a new realm, you generate a new tree. The old one is just... gone. No cleanup, no chunk unloading, no memory management. The function stops being evaluated.

Want me to spec out any of these components — the SDF tree compiler that generates wgsl, the BVH acceleration structure, the procedural dungeon generator that outputs SDF trees, or the creature parameterizer?

Is that truly the best we can do? This still feels like optimizing rather than innovating, and then how does the AI and combat tie into it? I want everything to be integrated, efficient, procedurally generated, and nigh-infinite. Do we have enough materials? Do the materials have enough dimensions/properties? What about physics and chemistry and magic? Is Rust the best language?

You're right to push. Everything I've said so far is still thinking in layers — rendering layer, simulation layer, AI layer, combat layer — bolted together with message passing. That's how every game engine works and it's why every game engine feels like a collection of systems pretending to be one thing.

Let me stop researching and start *thinking*.

Here's the idea that's been forming. I need to say this carefully because I think it might be the real thing.

Every game engine in existence — every single one — is a collection of systems that talk to each other. Rendering system. Physics system. AI system. Audio system. They share data through an ECS or a scene graph or message passing, but they are fundamentally separate machines that happen to look at the same entities. This is why "integration" is always a problem. The systems don't share a worldview. They share data structures.

What if IL didn't have systems at all? What if the entire game was **one mathematical object**?

Now your practical questions.

**Is Rust the right language?** Yes, but not for the reason you'd think. Rust isn't optimal because it's fast (C++ is equally fast). Rust is optimal because this architecture demands *two* languages working together, and Rust's ecosystem handles that better than anything else. The engine — the scheduler, the field evaluator, the BVH, the IO — lives in Rust. But the field itself — the composition of primitives, the evolution equations, the generation grammars — should be expressed in a **domain-specific language that compiles to GPU compute shaders (wgsl)**. Rust's procedural macro system and `wgpu`'s shader pipeline make this compilation step natural. You write the field DSL as a Rust proc-macro or as an interpreted tree that generates wgsl at runtime. The Rust engine manages execution; the DSL describes what exists.

This is how the demoscene works — the 64KB demos that produce entire worlds are effectively tiny compilers that generate shader code. IL would be a general-purpose version of that pattern.

**Do you have enough material dimensions?** 13 is not enough, and worse, discrete axes are the wrong abstraction entirely. Materials should be embeddings — points in a continuous space where proximity means similarity. Iron and steel are close together. Iron and wood are far apart. Mithril exists in a direction that no mundane material occupies — you literally cannot reach it by alloying or smelting, only by magic (moving through material-space along a path that crosses the "arcane barrier"). Transmutation isn't table lookup — it's navigation through a high-dimensional landscape. Alchemy is pathfinding in material-space.

The ~42 dimensions I sketched above are a starting point. Some of those will collapse (you might not need all 4 elemental alignment axes). Others will expand (the electromagnetic block might need more nuance for interesting visual effects). The right number emerges from playtesting.
```rust
pub struct DataLoader {
    /// Search paths in priority order (first match wins)
    /// Higher index = higher priority (overrides lower)
    search_paths: Vec<PathBuf>,
}

impl DataLoader {
    pub fn new(game_root: &Path) -> Self {
        let mut paths = vec![
            game_root.join("data"),           // Base game data (lowest priority)
        ];
        
        // Mod directories: alphabetical loading order within mods/
        let mods_dir = game_root.join("mods");
        if mods_dir.exists() {
            if let Ok(entries) = std::fs::read_dir(&mods_dir) {
                let mut mod_dirs: Vec<PathBuf> = entries
                    .filter_map(|e| e.ok())
                    .map(|e| e.path())
                    .filter(|p| p.is_dir())
                    .collect();
                mod_dirs.sort();
                paths.extend(mod_dirs);       // Mods override base data
            }
        }
        
        Self { search_paths: paths }
    }

    /// Find a file by relative path. Last match wins (highest priority).
    pub fn resolve(&self, relative: &str) -> Option<PathBuf> {
        self.search_paths.iter().rev()
            .map(|base| base.join(relative))
            .find(|p| p.exists())
    }

    /// Find ALL matching files (for merging, e.g., material databases)
    pub fn resolve_all(&self, relative: &str) -> Vec<PathBuf> {
        self.search_paths.iter()
            .map(|base| base.join(relative))
            .filter(|p| p.exists())
            .collect()
    }
}
```
